Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables

Shuyuan Chen    Yifan Cui ††thanks: Correspondence to cuiyf@zju.edu.cn.
Zhejiang University
Abstract

In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

keywords: Average treatment effect, Bridge function, Instrumented difference-in-differences, Invalid instrumental variable, Projection operator, Riesz representation

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

In many biomedical and econometric applications, unmeasured confounding remains a major obstacle to causal inference. Instrumental variable (IV) methods offer a principled approach to addressing this challenge by exploiting auxiliary variables to identify causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding (19; 2).

Despite their widespread use, classical IV methods rely on assumptions that can be difficult to justify in practice. A valid IV must satisfy three core assumptions, possibly conditional on observed covariates: (a) relevance, requiring an association between the IV and the treatment; (b) independence, requiring the IV to be independent of unmeasured confounders; and (c) the exclusion restriction, requiring the IV to affect the outcome only through the treatment. Weak instrument relevance can lead to unstable estimation and unreliable inference, whereas violations of independence or the exclusion restriction can invalidate identification and bias causal effect estimates.

These challenges have motivated a growing body of work on causal identification and estimation with invalid instruments. A recent review by Kang et al. (21) summarizes advances in causal identification and inference with instruments that violate the independence assumption or the exclusion restriction. Such methods are particularly relevant in applications where instrument validity is difficult to justify, including personalized pricing (24), human-machine interaction (15), and biomedical research (4; 46).

One line of work develops methods for estimation and inference on linear causal effects under assumptions about the composition of the candidate instrument set, without prior knowledge of which instruments are valid. Prominent examples include the majority rule (17; 20; 37) and the plurality rule (16; 38). The former requires more than half of the instruments to be valid, whereas the latter permits a smaller valid subset under additional conditions on the invalid instruments.

Another strand of work exploits heteroscedasticity for identification, including the approach of Lewbel (22) and the G-estimation under no interaction with unmeasured selection (GENIUS) (34; 32; 42). Rather than requiring a sufficiently large subset of valid instruments, GENIUS allows violations of the exclusion restriction under alternative structural assumptions. In particular, identification combines variation in the conditional treatment variance across instrument levels with a restriction requiring the conditional covariance between the treatment and the outcome residual to remain invariant across those levels.

More closely related to our work are semiparametric efficient G-estimators that identify effects in partially linear models without requiring prior knowledge of which instruments are valid (5; 6). Relaxations of proxy validity assumptions have also been studied in proximal causal inference (43). In a complementary direction, the instrumented difference-in-differences (IVDID) framework (41; 35; 45) exploits temporal variation to identify average treatment effects under assumptions that allow for violations of the exclusion restriction.

Finally, our work connects to Riesz learning, which provides tools for estimating Riesz representers and constructing orthogonal bias corrections (7; 9), and to nonparametric instrumental variable methods that study identification and estimation through conditional moment restrictions (27). It also connects to proximal causal inference, which identifies causal effects through bridge functions satisfying conditional moment restrictions (25; 12). Together, these connections motivate our operator-based perspective on causal identification and estimation.

1.2 Our contributions

In this paper, we develop a projected IV (PIV) framework that relaxes conventional identification assumptions for IVs. The key idea of the PIV approach is to interpret conditional expectations as projection operators on a suitable Hilbert space and replace the conditional expectation operator with a more general projection operator. Notably, under appropriate identification conditions, this framework can identify causal effects even when none of the candidate instruments satisfies the classical IV validity assumptions.

Our main contributions are fivefold. First, we propose the PIV framework from a novel operator-based perspective to identify the average treatment effect (ATE). Identification results for other estimands such as the counterfactual means and average treatment effect on the treated are given in the Appendix. Second, we provide an inverse problem interpretation of the proposed framework based on the Riesz representation. Third, we develop debiased and adaptive estimators using semiparametric efficiency theory. Fourth, we establish connections between invalid IV and IVDID through our PIV framework. Fifth, we examine how one can utilize invalid PIV for identification.

We outline the remainder of the paper as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the notions of PIV and projected regular weighting functions (PRWF). In Section 3, we interpret the proposed PIV condition from the perspectives of Riesz learning and inverse problems. In Section 4, we develop two estimators within the debiased machine learning framework. The first estimator directly employs a prespecified PRWF, while the second adaptively selects an optimal weighting function. We establish that both estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal, provided that the L2L_{2}-norm convergence rate of the nuisance function estimators is faster than n−1/4n^{-1/4}. Section 5 develops a novel application of the proposed PIV framework to invalid IV problems, whereas Section 6 clarifies its connections to the existing invalid IV literature. Finally, Section 7 presents simulation studies that illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods under a range of data-generating processes. Section 8 provides a real-data application, and Section 9 discusses extensions to invalid PIVs.

2 Projected IV framework

2.1 Toy Examples

We first introduce two toy examples to illustrate the main idea. Suppose that ZZ is a univariate continuous and bounded IV, and X=∅X=\emptyset. In these toy examples only, we allow the treatment AA to be continuous. For the first example, consider the following model where the IV exclusion restriction is violated

Y=β1o+βao​A+βzo​Z+ϵ,𝔼⁡[ϵ∣Z]=0.\displaystyle Y=\beta_{1}^{o}+\beta_{a}^{o}A+\beta_{z}^{o}Z+\epsilon,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid Z]=0.

The unmeasured confounder ϵ\epsilon can be correlated with the endogenous treatment variable AA, and our primary interest lies in identifying βao\beta_{a}^{o}. Under the standard IV framework, βao\beta_{a}^{o} is not identifiable when the exclusion restriction is violated, i.e., when βzo≠0\beta_{z}^{o}\neq 0. However, because the support of ZZ is sufficiently rich, the redundant information contained in different regions of the support can still be exploited.

Specifically, define 𝒮lm:={s∈L2(Z):s(Z)=θ1Z+θ0,θ0,θ1∈ℝ}¯\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}:=\overline{\{s\in L_{2}(Z):s(Z)=\theta_{1}Z+\theta_{0},\;\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\mathbb{R}\}}, and for any f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O), define 𝕊lm​[f]:=arg⁡mins∈𝒮lm⁡𝔼⁡[{f⁡(O)−s⁡(Z)}2].\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[f]:=\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}}\mathbb{E}[\{f(O)-s(Z)\}^{2}]. Then, for any π∈L2​(Z)\pi\in L_{2}(Z), it is easy to verify that

𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}​(Y−βao​A)]=βzo​𝔼​[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}​Z]+β1o​𝔼​[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}]=0,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}(Y-\beta_{a}^{o}A)\bigr]=\beta_{z}^{o}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}Z\bigr]+\beta_{1}^{o}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}\bigr]=0,

where the last equality follows from the fact that π−𝕊lm​[π]\pi-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi] is orthogonal to all the elements in 𝒮lm\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}. Thus, if there exists a π∈L2​(Z)\pi\in L_{2}(Z) such that 𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}​A]≠0\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}A\bigr]\neq 0, we can identify βao\beta_{a}^{o} by

βao=𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}​Y]/𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)}​A].\displaystyle\beta_{a}^{o}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}Y\bigr]/\mathbb{E}\bigl[\{\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\}A\bigr]. (2.1)

Notably, when ZZ is binary, π⁡(Z)−𝕊lm​[π]​(Z)≡0\pi(Z)-\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}[\pi](Z)\equiv 0, so the identification strategy fails. In general, ZZ must take at least three distinct values for identification to be possible.

2.2 The projection operator

To generalize the idea presented in Section 2.1, we introduce a proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Intuitively, 𝒮\mathcal{S} represents the allowable structure of 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X]. We formalize this notion below. By convention, we define Lp​(∅):=ℝL_{p}(\emptyset):=\mathbb{R} for p∈(1,∞]p\in(1,\infty].

Definition 2.1.

We say that 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X) if:

  1. (a)

    L2​(X)⊆𝒮⊆L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(X)\subseteq\mathcal{S}\subseteq L_{2}(Z,X), and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a closed linear subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X);

  2. (b)

    For any f1,f2∈𝒮f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{S} and any c1,c2∈L∞​(X)c_{1},c_{2}\in L_{\infty}(X), we have c1​f1+c2​f2∈𝒮;c_{1}f_{1}+c_{2}f_{2}\in\mathcal{S};

  3. (c)

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is equipped with the inherited inner product ⟨f1,f2⟩=𝔼⁡[f1​(Z,X)​f2​(Z,X)].\langle f_{1},f_{2}\rangle=\mathbb{E}[f_{1}(Z,X)f_{2}(Z,X)].

Here, “proper” denotes the properties in Definition 2.1; it does not mean a strict subset. Obviously, 𝒮lm\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}} and 𝒮qm\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{qm}} are both proper Hilbert subspaces of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X) when X=∅X=\emptyset. Also, L2​(X)L_{2}(X) itself is the smallest proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X). Next, define 𝕊:L2​(O)→𝒮\mathbb{S}:L_{2}(O)\to\mathcal{S} as a projection operator that maps any function f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O) onto the proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

𝕊⁡[f]:=arg⁡mins∈𝒮⁡𝔼⁡[{f⁡(O)−s⁡(Z,X)}2].\displaystyle\mathbb{S}[f]:=\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\{f(O)-s(Z,X)\right\}^{2}\right].

The projection operator 𝕊\mathbb{S} has the following properties, which are important for identification.

Proposition 1.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X).

  1. (a)

    For every f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O), 𝕊⁡[f]\mathbb{S}[f] is the unique function in 𝒮\mathcal{S} such that, for all s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S},

    𝔼⁡[{f⁡(O)−𝕊⁡[f]​(Z,X)}​s​(Z,X)∣X]=0.\mathbb{E}[\{f(O)-\mathbb{S}[f](Z,X)\}s(Z,X)\mid X]=0.
  2. (b)

    For all f1,f2∈L2​(O)f_{1},f_{2}\in L_{2}(O) and any c1,c2∈L∞​(X)c_{1},c_{2}\in L_{\infty}(X), 𝕊⁡[c1​f1+c2​f2]=c1​𝕊​[f1]+c2​𝕊​[f2]\mathbb{S}[c_{1}f_{1}+c_{2}f_{2}]=c_{1}\mathbb{S}[f_{1}]+c_{2}\mathbb{S}[f_{2}].

  3. (c)

    For any other proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime} of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X) with 𝒮⊆𝒮′\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\prime} and the corresponding projection operator 𝕊′\mathbb{S}^{\prime}, 𝕊⁡[f]=𝕊⁡[𝕊′​[f]]\mathbb{S}[f]=\mathbb{S}[\mathbb{S}^{\prime}[f]] for all f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O).

Proposition 1(a) establishes the uniqueness of 𝕊⁡[f]\mathbb{S}[f] and the orthogonality condition characterizing 𝕊⁡[f]\mathbb{S}[f] as the projection of ff onto 𝒮\mathcal{S}, conditional on XX. Proposition 1(b) demonstrates that 𝕊\mathbb{S} is a linear projection operator. Proposition 1(c) reflects the nesting property of orthogonal projections: projecting onto a smaller subspace is equivalent to first projecting onto a larger subspace and then projecting again onto the smaller one.

In particular, when taking 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X), we have 𝕊⁡[f]​(Z,X)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(O)∣X]\mathbb{S}[f](Z,X)=\mathbb{E}[f(O)\mid X], which corresponds to the conditional expectation operator. When we take 𝒮=L2​(Z,X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(Z,X), we obtain 𝕊[f](Z,X)=𝔼[f(O)∣Z,X]\mathbb{S}[f](Z,X)=\mathbb{E}[f(O)\mid Z,X].

2.3 Projected regular weighting function

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X). We propose the key concept of an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF, which controls variance and ensures the stability of the functionals proposed later for identification.

Definition 2.2 (𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF).

We say that π∈L2​(Z,X)\pi\in L_{2}(Z,X) is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-projected regular weighting function (PRWF) if there exists a constant ϵ0∈(0,1]\epsilon_{0}\in(0,1] such that |𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​A∣X]|≥ϵ0\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\right\}A\mid X\right]\right|\geq\epsilon_{0}, and 𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}2∣X]≤1/ϵ0\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\}^{2}\mid X]\leq 1/\epsilon_{0} almost surely.

Note that 𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}2∣X]≤1/ϵ0\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\}^{2}\mid X]\leq 1/\epsilon_{0} is satisfied for a uniformly bounded π\pi. Therefore, the existence of an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF depends critically on the IV relevance structure. Intuitively, when Z⟂⟂A|XZ\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid X, it is clear that no 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF can exist. Next, we introduce the notion of 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance, which formalizes the relevance structure between the IVs and the treatment.

Definition 2.3 (𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance).

Define π∗o(Z,X):=𝔼[A∣Z,X]\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{E}[A\mid Z,X]. We say that ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA if there exists an ϵ0∈(0,1]\epsilon_{0}\in(0,1] such that 𝔼⁡[{π∗o​(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π∗o]​(Z,X)}2|X]≥ϵ0\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi_{*}^{o}](Z,X)\right\}^{2}\middle|X\right]\geq\epsilon_{0} almost surely.

The definition of 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance measures IV strength via the L2L_{2}-distance between π∗o​(Z,X)\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X) and its projection onto 𝒮\mathcal{S}. As shown in the next proposition, this notion of IV relevance becomes increasingly stringent as the subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S} grows larger.

Proposition 2.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime} be two proper Hilbert subspaces of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X), where 𝒮⊆𝒮′\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\prime}. Then 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}-relevance implies 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance.

For the special case 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X), 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance implies that there exists a positive ϵ0\epsilon_{0}, such that E​[ {E[A ∣Z,X] - E[A ∣X]}^2 ∣X ]= Var​{ E[A ∣Z,X] ∣X }≥ϵ_0. This condition requires that the conditional treatment probability varies with ZZ given XX, recovering the IV relevance concept in Chen et al. (5). Next, we formalize the relation between the existence of 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF and the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance condition.

Proposition 3 (Existence of PRWF).

The following three statements are equivalent: (a) There exists an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF; (b) π∗o\pi_{*}^{o} is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF; (c) ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA.

Proposition 3 shows that an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF exists if and only if ZZ contains sufficient information about AA. Moreover, whenever such a function exists, the weighting function π∗o\pi_{*}^{o} is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF, thereby justifying its role as the canonical optimal weighting function.

2.4 Identification with PIV

In this subsection, we introduce another key concept of a PIV, which utilizes a proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

Definition 2.4 (𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV).

We say that ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV if (a) 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]∈𝒮\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X]\in\mathcal{S}; (b) For any π∈L2​(Z,X)\pi\in L_{2}(Z,X), Cov{A{π(Z,X)−𝕊[π](Z,X)},Y(1)−Y(0)∣X}=0\mathrm{Cov}\{A\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\},Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X\}=0 almost surely.

Definition 2.4(a) requires that the structure of 𝒮\mathcal{S} adequately captures the dependence of Y⁡(0)Y(0) on ZZ. In particular, when 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X), the condition requires 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X] to be invariant with respect to ZZ, which is a direct consequence of the IV independence condition when ZZ is valid.

Definition 2.4(b) serves as an orthogonality restriction, analogous to the no unmeasured common effect modifier assumption (10). Specifically, Definition 2.4(b) requires either that the individual treatment effect Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) be exogenous or that A​{π−𝕊⁡[π]}A\{\pi-\mathbb{S}[\pi]\} be conditionally uncorrelated with the component of Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) attributable to unmeasured confounding.

Example 2.1 (Linear model with constant treatment effect).

When X=∅X=\emptyset, consider 𝒮=𝒮lm\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}, as defined in Section 2.1. The linear model (20; 16; 5) assumes that Y⁡(a)=βo​a+θ0o+∑j=1dZθjo​Z[j]+ϵY(a)=\beta^{o}a+\theta_{0}^{o}+\sum_{j=1}^{d_{Z}}\theta_{j}^{o}Z_{[j]}+\epsilon, where 𝔼⁡[ϵ∣Z]=0.\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid Z]=0. In particular, 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(0)∣Z]=θ0o+∑j=1dZθjo​Z[j]∈𝒮lm,\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z]=\theta_{0}^{o}+\sum_{j=1}^{d_{Z}}\theta_{j}^{o}Z_{[j]}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lm}}, so that Definition 2.4(a) is satisfied. In addition, Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) is the constant βo\beta^{o}, so that Definition 2.4(b) is satisfied.

To understand the meaning of A​{π−𝕊⁡[π]}A\{\pi-\mathbb{S}[\pi]\} being conditionally uncorrelated with Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0), we provide an alternative description of Definition 2.4(b) when ZZ is exogenous and present two concrete examples. Let A⁡(z)A(z) denote the potential treatment value when the instrument is set to Z=zZ=z.

Proposition 4.

Suppose that {A⁡(z),Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)}⟂⟂Z|X\{A(z),Y(1)-Y(0)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid X, and define g(z,x):=Cov{A(z),Y(1)−Y(0)∣X=x}g(z,x):=\mathrm{Cov}\{A(z),Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x\}. Then, Definition 2.4(b) is equivalent to requiring that g∈𝒮g\in\mathcal{S}.

Example 2.2 (Mixture model with 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X)).

Suppose that Z⟂⟂(U,G)|XZ\perp\!\!\!\perp(U,G)\mid X, A⁡(z)=(1−G)​f0​(z,X)+G​f1​(U,X)A(z)=(1-G)f_{0}(z,X)+Gf_{1}(U,X), and Y⁡(a)=e⁡(a,U,X)Y(a)=e(a,U,X). Here, the ranges of f0f_{0}, f1f_{1} are 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and G∈{0,1}G\in\{0,1\} is a group indicator, satisfying G⟂⟂U|XG\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid X. One can verify that g⁡(z0,X)−g⁡(z0′,X)≡0g(z_{0},X)-g(z_{0}^{\prime},X)\equiv 0, since A⁡(z0)−A⁡(z0′)=(1−G)​{f0​(z0,X)−f0​(z0′,X)}A(z_{0})-A(z_{0}^{\prime})=(1-G)\{f_{0}(z_{0},X)-f_{0}(z_{0}^{\prime},X)\} is independent of Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)=e⁡(1,U,X)−e⁡(0,U,X)Y(1)-Y(0)=e(1,U,X)-e(0,U,X) conditional on XX. By Proposition 4, Definition 2.4(b) is satisfied for 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X).

Example 2.3 (Mixture model with 𝒮=∑j=1,2L2​(Z[j],X)¯\mathcal{S}=\overline{\sum_{j=1,2}L_{2}(Z_{[j]},X)}).

Suppose that Z⟂⟂(U,G)|XZ\perp\!\!\!\perp(U,G)\mid X, A⁡(z[1],z[2])=I⁡(G=0)​f0​(z[1],z[2],X)+I⁡(G=1)​f1​(U,z[1],X)+I⁡(G=2)​f2​(U,z[2],X),A(z_{[1]},z_{[2]})=I(G=0)f_{0}(z_{[1]},z_{[2]},X)+I(G=1)f_{1}(U,z_{[1]},X)+I(G=2)f_{2}(U,z_{[2]},X), and Y⁡(a)=e⁡(a,U,X)Y(a)=e(a,U,X). Here, the ranges of f0f_{0}, f1f_{1}, f2f_{2} are 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and G∈{0,1,2}G\in\{0,1,2\} is a group indicator satisfying G⟂⟂U|XG\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid X. Then, one can readily verify that g⁡(z[1],z[2],X)−g⁡(z[1]′,z[2],X)−g⁡(z[1],z[2]′,X)+g⁡(z[1]′,z[2]′,X)≡0g(z_{[1]},z_{[2]},X)-g(z_{[1]}^{\prime},z_{[2]},X)-g(z_{[1]},z_{[2]}^{\prime},X)+g(z_{[1]}^{\prime},z_{[2]}^{\prime},X)\equiv 0, indicating that g∈∑j=1,2L2​(Z[j],X)¯g\in\overline{\sum_{j=1,2}L_{2}(Z_{[j]},X)}. By Proposition 4, Definition 2.4(b) is satisfied for 𝒮=∑j=1,2L2​(Z[j],X)¯\mathcal{S}=\overline{\sum_{j=1,2}L_{2}(Z_{[j]},X)}.

In contrast to 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance, an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV is always an 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}-PIV for any two proper Hilbert subspaces with 𝒮⊆𝒮′\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\prime}. Consequently, choosing a larger 𝒮\mathcal{S} is more likely to violate the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance condition, leading to increased variance and instability, whereas choosing a smaller 𝒮\mathcal{S} is more likely to violate the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV condition, thereby invalidating the identifying formula. This highlights a bias-variance trade-off induced by the choice of 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

We now present identification with PIV in the following theorem.

Theorem 1 (Identification).

Suppose that ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV and π\pi is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF. Then 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]=ψ𝒮,πo\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}, where ψ𝒮,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o} is the following inverse probability weighting (IPW) functional:

ψ𝒮,πo:=𝔼⁡[π​(Z,X)−𝕊​[π]​(Z,X)𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​A|X]​Y].\displaystyle\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)}{\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\right\}A|X\right]}Y\right].
Remark 2.1.

If ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV and 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X), then Theorem 1 reduces to

𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]=𝔼⁡[π⁡(Z,X)−𝔼⁡[π⁡(Z,X)∣X]Cov{π(Z,X),A|X}​Y],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{E}[\pi(Z,X)\mid X]}{\mathrm{Cov}\left\{\pi(Z,X),\,A|X\right\}}Y\right],

a result established in Theorem 2.3 of Chen et al. (5) for valid IVs.

3 An inverse problem view

In this section, we develop an inverse problem interpretation of the PIV framework through treatment bridge functions (12) and outcome bridge functions (25), highlighting its connection to Riesz learning (7; 2). Specifically, we find a treatment bridge function q∈𝒮⟂q\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp} that satisfies

𝔼[q(Z,X)A|X]≡1 almost surely;𝔼[q(Z,X)2∣X]∈L∞(X).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[q(Z,X)A\middle|X\right]\equiv 1\text{ almost surely};\quad\mathbb{E}[q(Z,X)^{2}\mid X]\in L_{\infty}(X). (3.1)

Notably, Equation (3.1) was previously established by Chernozhukov et al. (7); Chernozhukov et al. (2) for the special case 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X). We next provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a solution to Equation (3.1).

Proposition 5 (Existence of treatment bridge).

There exists a solution q∈𝒮⟂q\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp} to Equation (3.1) if and only if ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA. In addition, for any 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF π\pi, q𝒮,π​(Z,X):=π​(Z,X)−𝕊​[π]​(Z,X)𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​A|X]q_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(Z,X):=\frac{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)}{\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\right\}A|X\right]} satisfies Equation (3.1).

Proposition 5 reveals a close connection between 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance and the solvability of Equation (3.1). In particular, by Proposition 3, q𝒮,π∗oq_{\mathcal{S},\pi_{*}^{o}} provides a natural candidate solution to the treatment bridge equation. Now, we can identify the ATE using a treatment bridge function.

Theorem 2 (Treatment bridge identification).

Suppose that ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV. Then, for any q∈𝒮⟂q\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp} satisfying Equation (3.1), 𝔼⁡[q⁡(Z,X)​Y]=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]\mathbb{E}\left[q(Z,X)Y\right]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)].

Remark 3.1.

Equation (3.1) may admit multiple solutions, each of which can be used for identification. Selecting an efficient q⁡(Z,X)q(Z,X), or combining multiple treatment bridge solutions to improve the efficiency of the proposed estimator, is an interesting direction for future research but lies beyond the scope of this paper.

Alternatively, we can also identify the ATE by constructing outcome bridge functions. We consider the problem of finding an outcome bridge function ho∈L2​(X)h^{o}\in L_{2}(X), such that

𝔼⁡[d⁡(Z,X)​{Y−A​ho​(X)}]=0,∀d∈𝒮⟂.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[d(Z,X)\{Y-Ah^{o}(X)\}\big]=0,\qquad\forall\,d\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp}. (3.2)

To establish the uniqueness of the solution to Equation (3.2), we introduce the definition of 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness.

Definition 3.1 (𝒮\mathcal{S}-Completeness).

We say that 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness holds if for any g∈L2​(X)g\in L_{2}(X), g⁡(X)≡0g(X)\equiv 0 if and only if for all d∈𝒮⟂d\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp}, 𝔼⁡[d⁡(Z,X)​A​g​(X)]=0\mathbb{E}\!\left[d(Z,X)A\,g(X)\right]=0.

Note that the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness condition is a weaker form of the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance condition. Now, we can establish identification of the ATE using the solution to Equation (3.2) and 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness.

Theorem 3 (Outcome bridge identification).

(a) If there exists a solution q∈𝒮⟂q\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp} to Equation (3.1), then 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness holds. (b) If Equation (3.2) admits a solution and 𝒮\mathcal{S}-completeness holds, then the solution is unique. (c) If ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV for AA, then ho​(X)=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣X]h^{o}(X)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X\right] is a solution to Equation (3.2).

Theorem 3 shows that we can first find a solution ho​(X)h^{o}(X) to Equation (3.2), and then identify the ATE by 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]=𝔼⁡[ho​(X)]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\mathbb{E}[h^{o}(X)] if this solution is unique. Figure 3.1 provides an overview of the key ideas and identification results developed in this section.

4 Semiparametric analysis

4.1 Debiased estimator with a fixed PRWF

In this subsection, we present semiparametric analysis for ψ𝒮,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o} when a prespecified proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S} and a corresponding 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF π\pi are given. In particular, define a nuisance vector as α𝒮,πo=[δ𝒮o,η𝒮o,ρ𝒮,πo,κ𝒮,πo,μ𝒮,πo]\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}=[\delta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o},\eta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o},\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o},\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o},\mu_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}], where

δ𝒮o​(Z,X):=𝕊⁡[A]​(Z,X),η𝒮o​(Z,X):=𝕊⁡[Y]​(Z,X),ρ𝒮,πo​(Z,X):=𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X),\displaystyle\delta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X),\qquad\eta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{S}[Y](Z,X),\qquad\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X),
κ𝒮,πo​(X):=𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​{A−𝕊⁡[A]​(Z,X)}∣X],\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(X):=\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\}\{A-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}\mid X],
μ𝒮,πo​(X):=𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​{Y−𝕊⁡[Y]​(Z,X)}∣X]𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊⁡[π]​(Z,X)}​{A−𝕊⁡[A]​(Z,X)}∣X].\displaystyle\mu_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(X):=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\}\{Y-\mathbb{S}[Y](Z,X)\}\mid X]}{\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}[\pi](Z,X)\}\{A-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}\mid X]}.

By the definitions of nuisance functions, it can be readily verified that

ψ𝒮,πo=𝔼⁡[π⁡(Z,X)−ρ𝒮,πo​(Z,X)κ𝒮,πo​(X)​Y]=𝔼⁡[μ𝒮,πo​(X)].\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\pi(Z,X)-\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(Z,X)}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(X)}\,Y\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mu_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}(X)\right].

The former representation resembles an IPW functional, whereas the latter is analogous to an outcome regression (OR) functional. Next, we derive the efficient influence function (EIF) of ψ𝒮,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}.

Theorem 4 (EIF).

Suppose that π\pi is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF. Under the differentiability conditions in Lemma E.1 (see the Appendix for details), the EIF of ψ𝒮,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o} in the nonparametric model is

φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ𝒮,π,α𝒮,π)=π⁡(Z,X)−ρ𝒮,π​(Z,X)κ𝒮,π​(X)​{Y−η𝒮​(Z,X)}\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi})=\dfrac{\pi(Z,X)-\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(Z,X)}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(X)}\left\{Y-\eta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X)\right\}
+μ𝒮,π​(X)​(1−{π⁡(Z,X)−ρ𝒮,π​(Z,X)}​{A−δ𝒮​(Z,X)}κ𝒮,π​(X))−ψ𝒮,π.\displaystyle+\mu_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(X)\left(1-\dfrac{\left\{\pi(Z,X)-\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(Z,X)\right\}\left\{A-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X)\right\}}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(X)}\right)-\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}.
Remark 4.1.

The efficiency analysis in this section is carried out relative to the nonparametric model. The semiparametric theory developed by Dong et al. (13) for the case 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X) could potentially be adapted to extend the semiparametric efficiency analysis of the proposed framework.

Since all 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWFs can be adopted to identify the ATE, we are interested in selecting an optimal weighting function. We define Ψo​(X):=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣X]\Psi^{o}(X):=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X], and demonstrate that π∗o\pi_{*}^{o} is a good candidate.

Proposition 6 (Lower efficiency bound).

Suppose that ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV that is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA, and

𝔼[{Y−AΨo(X)−𝕊[Y−AΨo](Z,X)}2|Z,X]⟂⟂Z∣X.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{Y-A\Psi^{o}(X)-\mathbb{S}[Y-A\Psi^{o}](Z,X)\right\}^{2}\middle|Z,X\right]\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid X. (4.1)

Then 𝔼⁡[φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ𝒮,πo,α𝒮,πo)2]\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o})^{2}\right] achieves its lower bound when taking π=π∗o\pi=\pi_{*}^{o}, provided that the influence functions being compared have finite second moments.

Remark 4.2.

The weighting functions that achieve the lower bound in Proposition 6 are not unique, since the asymptotic variance 𝔼⁡[φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ𝒮,πo,α𝒮,πo)2]\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o})^{2}\right] induced by π⁡(Z,X)=π∗o​(Z,X)​f​(X)+g⁡(X)\pi(Z,X)=\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X)f(X)+g(X) is the same as that induced by π∗o​(Z,X)\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X) for all choices such that π\pi remains an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF.

The conditional independence condition in (4.1) can be interpreted as a generalized homoskedasticity assumption. Specifically, after removing both the conditional treatment effect component A​Ψo​(X)A\Psi^{o}(X) and the projected component 𝕊⁡[Y−A​Ψo]​(Z,X)\mathbb{S}[Y-A\Psi^{o}](Z,X), the remaining residual variation is assumed not to depend on ZZ conditional on XX. Under this condition, π∗o​(Z,X)\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X) minimizes the asymptotic variance within the stated class of fixed-weight functionals. This comparison does not establish the efficiency bound in the smaller causal model defined by the PIV restrictions.

4.2 Adaptive estimator with optimal PRWF

In practice, it is unclear how to optimally select an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF π\pi when ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA. Propositions 3 and 6 motivate the choice of π∗o\pi_{*}^{o}. However, its true form is generally unknown, and directly utilizing a plug-in estimator π^∗\hat{\pi}_{*} may introduce non-negligible estimation bias. A principled approach to address this challenge is to treat π∗o\pi_{*}^{o} as a nuisance function and estimate it adaptively from the data. In particular, suppose that ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA. The parameter of interest is defined as

ψ𝒮,∗o:=𝔼⁡[𝔼[A|Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)𝔼[{𝔼[A|Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)}2|X]​Y].\displaystyle\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}[A|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)}{\mathbb{E}\left[\{\mathbb{E}[A|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}^{2}|X\right]}Y\right].

If ZZ is also an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV, then ψ𝒮,∗o=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)] by setting π=π∗o\pi=\pi_{*}^{o} in Theorem 1.

The unified nuisance function vector α𝒮,∗o:=[π∗o,δ𝒮o,ξ∗o,η𝒮o,κ𝒮,∗o,μ𝒮,∗o]\alpha_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}:=[\pi_{*}^{o},\delta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o},\xi_{*}^{o},\eta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o},\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o},\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}] includes

π∗o(Z,X):=𝔼[A∣Z,X],δ𝒮o(Z,X):=𝕊[A](Z,X),\displaystyle\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{E}[A\mid Z,X],\quad\delta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X),
ξ∗o(Z,X):=𝔼[Y∣Z,X],η𝒮o(Z,X):=𝕊[Y](Z,X),\displaystyle\xi_{*}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z,X],\quad\eta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o}(Z,X):=\mathbb{S}[Y](Z,X),
κ𝒮,∗o(X):=𝔼[{𝔼[A|Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)}2∣X],\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X):=\mathbb{E}[\{\mathbb{E}[A|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}^{2}\mid X],
μ𝒮,∗o​(X):=𝔼[{𝔼[A|Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)}{𝔼[Y|Z,X]−𝕊[Y](Z,X)}∣X]𝔼[{𝔼[A|Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)}2∣X].\displaystyle\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X):=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}[\{\mathbb{E}[A|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}\{\mathbb{E}[Y|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[Y](Z,X)\}\mid X]}{\mathbb{E}[\{\mathbb{E}[A|Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}^{2}\mid X]}.

We now present a semiparametric analysis of ψ𝒮,∗o\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}.

Theorem 5 (EIF).

If ZZ is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA, then, under the differentiability conditions in Lemma E.1, the EIF of ψ𝒮,∗o\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} in the nonparametric model is

φ𝒮,∗​(O,ψ𝒮,∗,α𝒮,∗)=1κ𝒮,∗​(X)​{(A−π∗​(Z,X))​ξ∗​(Z,X)−(A−δ𝒮​(Z,X))​η𝒮​(Z,X)}\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{S},*}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},*},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},*})=\frac{1}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}(X)}\left\{(A-\pi_{*}(Z,X))\xi_{*}(Z,X)-(A-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X))\eta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X)\right\}
+π∗​(Z,X)−δ𝒮​(Z,X)κ𝒮,∗​(X)​Y+μ𝒮,∗​(X)κ𝒮,∗​(X)​{κ𝒮,∗​(X)+(A−π∗​(Z,X))2−(A−δ𝒮​(Z,X))2}−ψ𝒮,∗.\displaystyle+\frac{\pi_{*}(Z,X)-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X)}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}(X)}Y+\dfrac{\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}(X)}{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}(X)}\left\{\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}(X)+(A-\pi_{*}(Z,X))^{2}-(A-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X))^{2}\right\}-\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}.

Compared with Theorem 4, Theorem 5 only requires the 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevance condition, which avoids prespecifying a known 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF. Moreover, the following proposition establishes the efficiency optimality of the adaptive estimator.

Proposition 7.

If ZZ is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PIV for AA and is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-relevant to AA, then 𝔼⁡[φ𝒮,∗​(O,ψ𝒮,∗o,α𝒮,∗o)2]=𝔼⁡[φ𝒮,π∗o​(O,ψ𝒮,π∗oo,α𝒮,π∗oo)2]\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},*}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi_{*}^{o}}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi_{*}^{o}}^{o},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi_{*}^{o}}^{o})^{2}].

Proposition 7 shows that under the restriction of Equation (4.1), the adaptive estimator attains the minimum asymptotic variance characterized in Proposition 6. Because the optimal choice π∗o\pi_{*}^{o} is generally unknown in practice, we use the adaptive procedure associated with ψ𝒮,∗o\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} as our default approach to estimating the ATE and constructing the corresponding confidence intervals.

4.3 Asymptotic theory

To reduce overfitting bias arising from nuisance function estimation and to relax empirical process conditions, we employ a KK-fold cross-fitting procedure (30; 6). Specifically, we partition the data into KK folds {Ik}k=1K\{I_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, where KK is fixed and |Ik|=n/K|I_{k}|=n/K (for simplicity, assume that KK divides nn). For each fold kk, the nuisance functions are estimated using observations in the complement I−k:={1,…,n}∖IkI_{-k}:=\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus I_{k}, yielding estimators α^𝒮,π(n,−k)\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{(n,-k)} and α^𝒮,∗(n,−k)\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}. For any integrable function ff, write 𝔼n​k​[f⁡(O)]:=|Ik|−1​∑i∈Ikf⁡(Oi)\mathbb{E}_{nk}[f(O)]:=|I_{k}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_{k}}f(O_{i}). The estimators ψ^𝒮,π\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},\pi} and ψ^𝒮,∗\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},*} are defined as the solutions to the following estimating equations:

1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ^𝒮,π,α^𝒮,π(n,−k))]=0;1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[φ𝒮,∗​(O,ψ^𝒮,∗,α^𝒮,∗(n,−k))]=0.\displaystyle\dfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}\left(O;\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{(n,-k)}\right)\right]=0;\quad\dfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},*}\left(O;\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},*},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}\right)\right]=0.

The estimated asymptotic variances of n​(ψ^𝒮,π−ψ𝒮,πo)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}-\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o}) and n​(ψ^𝒮,∗−ψ𝒮,∗o)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},*}-\psi_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}) are given by

(σ^𝒮,π)2\displaystyle(\hat{\sigma}_{\mathcal{S},\pi})^{2} :=1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ^𝒮,π,α^𝒮,π(n,−k))2];(σ^𝒮,∗)2:=1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[φ𝒮,∗​(O,ψ^𝒮,∗,α^𝒮,∗(n,−k))2].\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\!\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}\!\left(O;\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{(n,-k)}\right)^{2}\right];\quad(\hat{\sigma}_{\mathcal{S},*})^{2}:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\!\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},*}\!\left(O;\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S},*},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}\right)^{2}\right].

To mitigate the bias induced by plugging in estimated nuisance functions, we next establish the mixed bias property (29) of the proposed cross-fitted estimator. Specifically, we show that its bias decomposes into products of nuisance estimation errors and therefore has a second-order bias structure under mild regularity conditions.

Proposition 8 (Mixed bias property).

Suppose that π\pi is an 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWF for AA. For any α𝒮,π=[δ𝒮,η𝒮,ρ𝒮,π,κ𝒮,π,μ𝒮,π]\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi}=[\delta_{\mathcal{S}},\eta_{\mathcal{S}},\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\kappa_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\mu_{\mathcal{S},\pi}] with δ𝒮,η𝒮,ρ𝒮,π∈𝒮\delta_{\mathcal{S}},\eta_{\mathcal{S}},\rho_{\mathcal{S},\pi}\in\mathcal{S}, 𝔼⁡[φ𝒮,π​(O,ψ𝒮,πo,α𝒮,π)]\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}(O;\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o},\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi})] equals

4.4 Nuisance function estimation

In this subsection, we provide guidance on estimating the nuisance functions κ𝒮,∗o\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} and μ𝒮,∗o\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}, which depend on other nuisance functions and therefore require estimated pseudo outcomes when fitted by least squares regression. In particular, define Γ𝒮,∗o(X)=𝔼[{𝔼[A∣Z,X]−𝕊[A](Z,X)}{Y−𝕊[Y](Z,X)}∣X].\Gamma_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X)=\mathbb{E}[\{\mathbb{E}[A\mid Z,X]-\mathbb{S}[A](Z,X)\}\{Y-\mathbb{S}[Y](Z,X)\}\mid X]. We estimate μ𝒮,∗o\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} using the identity μ𝒮,∗o​(X)=Γ𝒮,∗o​(X)/κ𝒮,∗o​(X)\mu_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X)=\Gamma_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X)/\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}(X).

The definitions of Γ𝒮,∗o\Gamma_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} and κ𝒮,∗o\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} rely on the remaining nuisance functions in α𝒮,∗o\alpha_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}. Therefore, we utilize the orthogonal statistical learning framework (3) to mitigate the bias induced by using estimated nuisance functions to estimate Γ𝒮,∗o\Gamma_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o} and κ𝒮,∗o\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}. In particular, for each training sample I−kI_{-k}, we split the observations into LL equally sized folds {Ik​l}l=1L\{I_{kl}\}_{l=1}^{L} and estimate π^∗(n,−k​l)\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)}, δ^𝒮(n,−k​l)\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)}, ξ^∗(n,−k​l)\hat{\xi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)} and η^𝒮(n,−k​l)\hat{\eta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)} using the observations in I−k​l:=I−k\Ik​lI_{-kl}:=I_{-k}\backslash I_{kl}. Then, define two augmented squared loss functions

ℒκ​(O,κ,δ𝒮,π∗):=12​{(A−δ𝒮​(Z,X))2−(A−π∗​(Z,X))2−κ⁡(X)}2;\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(O;\kappa,\delta_{\mathcal{S}},\pi_{*}):=\frac{1}{2}\{(A-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X))^{2}-(A-\pi_{*}(Z,X))^{2}-\kappa(X)\}^{2};
ℒΓ​(O,Γ,δ𝒮,π∗,η𝒮,ξ∗):=12​{(A−π∗​(Z,X))​ξ∗​(Z,X)−(A−δ𝒮​(Z,X))​η𝒮​(Z,X)+(π∗​(Z,X)−δ𝒮​(Z,X))​Y−Γ⁡(X)}2.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}(O;\Gamma,\delta_{\mathcal{S}},\pi_{*},\eta_{\mathcal{S}},\xi_{*}):=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}(A-\pi_{*}(Z,X))\xi_{*}(Z,X)-(A-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X))\eta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X)\\ +(\pi_{*}(Z,X)-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}(Z,X))Y-\Gamma(X)\end{array}\right\}^{2}.

Let ℱκ\mathcal{F}_{\kappa} and ℱΓ\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma} be two prespecified function classes. For any integrable function ff, write 𝔼n​k​l​[f⁡(O)]:=|Ik​l|−1​∑i∈Ik​lf⁡(Oi)\mathbb{E}_{nkl}[f(O)]:=|I_{kl}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_{kl}}f(O_{i}). Then, κ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)\hat{\kappa}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)} and Γ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)\hat{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)} can be estimated by

κ^𝒮,∗(n,−k):=arg⁡minκ∈ℱκ​{1L​∑l=1L𝔼n​k​l​[ℒκ​(O,κ,δ^𝒮(n,−k​l),π^∗(n,−k​l))]};\displaystyle\hat{\kappa}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}:=\underset{\kappa\in\mathcal{F}_{\kappa}}{\arg\min}\left\{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{nkl}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}(O;\kappa,\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)},\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)})\right]\right\};
Γ^𝒮,∗(n,−k):=arg⁡minΓ∈ℱΓ​{1L​∑l=1L𝔼n​k​l​[ℒΓ​(O,Γ,δ^𝒮(n,−k​l),π^∗(n,−k​l),η^𝒮(n,−k​l),ξ^∗(n,−k​l))]}.\displaystyle\hat{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}:=\underset{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma}}{\arg\min}\left\{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{nkl}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}(O;\Gamma,\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)},\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)},\hat{\eta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)},\hat{\xi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)})\right]\right\}.

Theorem 8 (Convergence rate of nuisance estimators).

‖κ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)−κ𝒮,∗o‖22≲cn,κ2+log⁡(1/ϵ)n+∑l=1L{‖π^∗(n,−k​l)−π∗o‖44+‖δ^𝒮(n,−k​l)−δ𝒮o‖44};\displaystyle\|\hat{\kappa}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}-\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim c_{n,\kappa}^{2}+\frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{n}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left\{\|\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)}-\pi_{*}^{o}\|_{4}^{4}+\|\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)}-\delta_{\mathcal{S}}^{o}\|_{4}^{4}\right\};

To achieve the op(n−1/4)o_{p}(n^{-1/4}) convergence rates of ‖Γ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)−Γ𝒮,∗o‖2\|\hat{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}-\Gamma_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}\|_{2} and ‖κ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)−κ𝒮,∗o‖2\|\hat{\kappa}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}-\kappa_{\mathcal{S},*}^{o}\|_{2}, it suffices to require o(n−1/4)o(n^{-1/4}) convergence rates of the critical radii of ℱκ\mathcal{F}_{\kappa} and ℱΓ\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma}, and op(n−1/8)o_{p}(n^{-1/8}) convergence rates of L4L_{4} norms of π^∗(n,−k​l)\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)}, δ^𝒮(n,−k​l)\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)}, ξ^∗(n,−k​l)\hat{\xi}_{*}^{(n,-kl)}, and η^𝒮(n,−k​l)\hat{\eta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-kl)}. The procedure for estimating the nuisance functions in α𝒮,πo\alpha_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o} can be established similarly and is therefore omitted.

5 Application to invalid IV

5.1 Identifying assumptions

To illustrate the applicability of our proposed PIV framework, we consider an invalid IV setting. First, we define ⟨dZ⟩:={1,…,dZ}\langle d_{Z}\rangle:=\{1,\dots,d_{Z}\}, and let ν⊆⟨dZ⟩\nu\subseteq\langle d_{Z}\rangle be any subset with distinct indices. Let |ν||\nu| denote the cardinality of ν\nu. Define Z[ν]:={Z[j]}j∈νZ_{[\nu]}:=\{Z_{[j]}\}_{j\in\nu} and Z[−ν]:={Z[j]}j∉νZ_{[-\nu]}:=\{Z_{[j]}\}_{j\notin\nu}. The following assumptions are stated with respect to a non-empty candidate index set ν0⊆⟨dZ⟩\nu_{0}\subseteq\langle d_{Z}\rangle.

Assumption 5.1 (IV independence).

Z[ν0]⟂⟂U|Z[−ν0],XZ_{[\nu_{0}]}\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X.

Assumption 5.2 (Strong latent ignorability).

Y⁡(a)⟂⟂{A,Z[ν0]}|U,Z[−ν0],XY(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp\{A,Z_{[\nu_{0}]}\}\mid U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}.

Assumption 5.2′ (Weak latent ignorability).

𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)|A,U,Z,X]⟂⟂{A,Z[ν0]}∣U,Z[−ν0],X\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)|A,U,Z,X]\perp\!\!\!\perp\{A,Z_{[\nu_{0}]}\}\mid U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X.

Assumption 5.3 (ZZ-invariant treatment effect).

𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)∣Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂Z[−ν0]∣X\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}\mid X.

Assumption 5.4.

At least one of the following conditions holds:

  1. (a)

    (Additive IV) For some γ∈{1,…,|ν0|}\gamma\in\{1,\ldots,|\nu_{0}|\}, there exist {bν(U,Z[−ν],X):ν⊆ν0,|ν|=γ}\{b_{\nu}(U,Z_{[-\nu]},X):\nu\subseteq\nu_{0},\ |\nu|=\gamma\} and c⁡(Z,X)c(Z,X) such that Pr⁡(A=1|Z,U,X)=∑ν⊆ν0,|ν|=γbν​(U,Z[−ν],X)+c⁡(Z,X).\Pr(A=1\mid Z,U,X)=\sum_{\nu\subseteq\nu_{0},|\nu|=\gamma}b_{\nu}(U,Z_{[-\nu]},X)+c(Z,X).

  2. (b)

    (UU-invariant conditional treatment effect) 𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)∣U,Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂U∣Z[−ν0],X\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X.

If condition (b) holds, define γ†​(ν0)=|ν0|\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0})=|\nu_{0}|. Otherwise, define γ†​(ν0)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}) as the largest γ∈{1,…,|ν0|}\gamma\in\{1,\ldots,|\nu_{0}|\} for which condition (a) holds.

Remark 5.1.

As shown in Proposition 11 of Appendix C, under Assumption 5.3, γ†\gamma_{\dagger} is nondecreasing with respect to set inclusion: ν1⊆ν2\nu_{1}\subseteq\nu_{2} implies γ†​(ν1)≤γ†​(ν2).\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{1})\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{2}).

Assumption 5.1 states that Z[ν0]Z_{[\nu_{0}]} is independent of the unmeasured confounders UU, conditional on Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]} and XX. Assumption 5.2 can be interpreted as a latent IV ignorability condition that accounts for unmeasured confounding effects through UU. Assumption 5.3 imposes that 𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)∣Z[−ν0],X]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X] does not depend on Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}.

However, despite the simplicity and interpretability of Assumption 5.2, it can be relaxed to Assumption 5.2′, which only requires that 𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)∣A,U,Z,X]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid A,U,Z,X] does not depend on A,Z[ν0]A,Z_{[\nu_{0}]}, and is therefore strictly weaker than Assumption 5.2. For example, suppose that Assumption 5.1 holds for ν0=⟨dZ⟩\nu_{0}=\langle d_{Z}\rangle, and that the potential outcomes are generated, for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, as Y(a)=af(X) + e_0(U,X)+∑_j=1^d_Ze_j(U,X)g_j(Z_[j],X)+ϵ, with 𝔼[ϵ|Z,U,X]=0\mathbb{E}[\epsilon|Z,U,X]=0. In this setting, Assumption 5.2′ holds for ν0=⟨dZ⟩\nu_{0}=\langle d_{Z}\rangle, whereas non-constant direct effects of ZZ on the potential outcomes can violate Assumption 5.2.

Assumption 5.4 offers two alternative identification routes, since it suffices for either condition to hold. On the one hand, Assumption 5.4(a) imposes an additive structure of the treatment assignment mechanism, in which conditional on Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]} and XX, the treatment probability admits a decomposition in which each term involving UU depends on at most |ν0|−γ†​(ν0)|\nu_{0}|-\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}) components of Z[ν0]Z_{[\nu_{0}]}. This relaxes the additive IV structure in Wang and Tchetgen Tchetgen (36); Cui et al. (11); Hartwig et al. (18); Michael et al. (26). On the other hand, Assumption 5.4(b) requires that 𝔼[Y(1)−Y(0)∣U,Z[−ν0],X]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X] be invariant to UU. When ν0=⟨dZ⟩\nu_{0}=\langle d_{Z}\rangle, this reduces to the no additive UU-YY interaction condition of Wooldridge (40); Wang and Tchetgen Tchetgen (36); Hartwig et al. (18).

For illustration, we present three causal graphs in Figure 5.1, where X=∅X=\emptyset and Assumption 5.1 is always satisfied. Note that Figure 5.1(b) allows an association between UU and Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}. Moreover, all three causal graphs allow Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]} to have a direct effect on Y⁡(0)Y(0), thereby relaxing the classical exclusion restriction. When only the solid arrows are present, Assumption 5.2 is satisfied. However, in Figures 5.1(a) and (b), once the dashed arrows in Figure 5.1 are introduced, Assumption 5.2 may fail while Assumption 5.2′ still holds, highlighting the latter’s weaker requirements.

In addition, under the causal structure illustrated in Figure 5.1(a), Assumption 5.3 remains valid while still permitting interactions between the latent confounder UU and the treatment effect Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0). In Figure 5.1(b), both Assumptions 5.3 and 5.4(b) are satisfied, allowing interactions between Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]} and UU in the treatment assignment mechanism. This demonstrates that our invalid IV setting permits either UU-Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]} interactions or UU-Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) interactions, but not both simultaneously, under which Assumption 5.3 may fail to hold.

5.2 Causal identification

We now focus on a principled projection space induced by additive model structures. Let γ∈{0,…,dZ}\gamma\in\{0,\ldots,d_{Z}\} be a nonnegative integer, and define 𝒮γ:=∑ν:|ν|≥γL2(Z[−ν],X)¯.\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}:=\overline{\sum_{\nu:|\nu|\geq\gamma}L_{2}(Z_{[-\nu]},X)}. The space 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} consists of all functions that can be represented as additive combinations of components depending on Z[−ν]Z_{[-\nu]} and XX for subsets ν\nu satisfying |ν|≥γ|\nu|\geq\gamma, together with their limits in L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X). It is straightforward to verify that 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} is a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X). Moreover, 𝒮γ⊆𝒮γ′\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{\gamma^{\prime}} whenever γ≥γ′\gamma\geq\gamma^{\prime}. Define 𝕊γ:L2​(O)→𝒮γ\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}:L_{2}(O)\to\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} as a projection operator that maps f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O) onto 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}. When γ=dZ\gamma=d_{Z}, it can be verified that 𝒮dZ=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}_{d_{Z}}=L_{2}(X), and hence 𝕊dZ​[f]​(X)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(O)∣X]\mathbb{S}_{d_{Z}}[f](X)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(O)\mid X\right]. Additionally, when γ=0\gamma=0, it can be verified that 𝒮0=L2​(Z,X)\mathcal{S}_{0}=L_{2}(Z,X), and 𝕊0[f](Z,X)=𝔼[f(O)∣Z,X]\mathbb{S}_{0}[f](Z,X)=\mathbb{E}[f(O)\mid Z,X].

We next present a key lemma that connects the 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV framework to the invalid IV setting.

Lemma 5.1.

(a) Suppose that Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, then

𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]⟂⟂Z[ν0]∣Z[−ν0],X.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X]\perp\!\!\!\perp Z_{[\nu_{0}]}\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X. (5.1)

Consequently, Definition 2.4(a) is satisfied for 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} for all γ≤|ν0|\gamma\leq|\nu_{0}|. (b) Suppose that Assumptions 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, and 5.4 hold for ν0\nu_{0}. Then, Definition 2.4(b) is satisfied for 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} for all γ≤γ†​(ν0)\gamma\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}).

Notably, Equation (5.1) is actually required by Sun et al. (5) for some non-empty ν0\nu_{0}. Under Assumption 5.1, Assumption 5.2 implies this restriction. In turn, this restriction implies Definition 2.4(a) for 𝒮|ν0|\mathcal{S}_{|\nu_{0}|}, while the reverse implications do not hold in general.

Moreover, if Definition 2.4(a) holds for 𝒮γ1\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{1}} and Definition 2.4(b) holds for 𝒮γ2\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{2}}, then ZZ is an 𝒮min⁡{γ1,γ2}\mathcal{S}_{\min\{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\}}-PIV. Lemma 5.1 provides sufficient conditions for parts (a) and (b) of Definition 2.4, respectively. Combining these observations yields the following sufficient conditions under which ZZ is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV.

Proposition 9.

(a) If Assumptions 5.1–5.4 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, then, ZZ is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV for all γ≤γ†​(ν0)\gamma\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}).
(b) Let γ∗\gamma_{*} be the maximal number such that Definition 2.4(a) holds for 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}, i.e., 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]∈𝒮γ\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X]\in\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}. If Assumptions 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, 5.4 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, then ZZ is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV for all γ≤min⁡{γ∗,γ†​(ν0)}\gamma\leq\min\{\gamma_{*},\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0})\}.

By Lemma 5.1(a), we have γ∗≥|ν0|\gamma_{*}\geq|\nu_{0}|, so Proposition 9(a) follows directly from Proposition 9(b). Proposition 9(b) also shows that identification can be achieved even when Assumption 5.2 fails, provided Assumption 5.2′ holds. The admissible range of γ\gamma is constrained by both γ∗\gamma_{*} and γ†​(ν0)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}).

To characterize the largest attainable value of γ\gamma such that the 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV conditions hold, we define an index set ν0⊆⟨dZ⟩\nu_{0}\subseteq\langle d_{Z}\rangle to be regular if Assumptions 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, and 5.4 hold relative to ν0\nu_{0}. In Appendix C, under Assumption C.1, we show that the union of any two regular sets is still regular, indicating that the maximal regular set that contains all regular index sets is unique. We therefore define the unique largest regular index set νmax:=⋃ν0:ν0​ is regularν0\nu_{\max}:=\bigcup_{\nu_{0}:\,\nu_{0}\text{ is regular}}\nu_{0}, and define γmax:=min⁡{γ∗,γ†​(νmax)}\gamma_{\max}:=\min\{\gamma_{*},\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{\max})\} as the largest value of γ\gamma certified by these sufficient conditions.

Remark 5.2.

Because Assumption 5.2 implies Assumption 5.2′, νmax\nu_{\max} contains the indices of all IVs satisfying Assumptions 5.1–5.4, and there are no more than min⁡{γ∗,|νmax|}\min\{\gamma_{*},|\nu_{\max}|\} such IVs. In particular, if Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) is constant, the same containment and cardinality conclusions hold for all valid IVs satisfying Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2.

Figure 5.2 graphically represents the feasible region of γ\gamma for the identification of ATE, while values of γ\gamma that are too small or too large may lead to a violation of the 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-relevance or 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV condition, respectively. The following corollary summarizes the identification result and follows directly from Theorem 1 and Proposition 9.

Corollary 5.1.

If π\pi is an 𝒮γmax\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{\max}}-PRWF, then 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)]=ψ𝒮γmax,πo.\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\psi_{\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{\max}},\pi}^{o}.

Notably, when X=∅X=\emptyset, Sun et al. (5) require the existence of at least one 𝒮γmax\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{\max}}-PRWF in the class {∏j∈νZ[j]:|ν|≥dZ−γmax+1}\{\prod_{j\in\nu}Z_{[j]}:|\nu|\geq d_{Z}-\gamma_{\max}+1\}. By Proposition 3, this requirement is generally stronger than the 𝒮γmax\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{\max}}-relevance condition; the two conditions are equivalent when all IVs are binary.

For simplicity, we focus on the ATE throughout the main text. In Appendix A, we extend our approach to identify mean potential outcomes and the average treatment effect on the treated.

6 Connections to existing literature

6.1 IVDID

We first suppose that Z={Z[1],Z[2]}Z=\{Z_{[1]},Z_{[2]}\}, where Z[1],Z[2]∈{0,1}Z_{[1]},Z_{[2]}\in\{0,1\} are binary variables, and that ZZ is an 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}-PIV. In this setting, the IVDID functional studied in Ye et al. (41) is a special case of our functional ψ𝒮,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{o} with 𝒮=𝒮1\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{1} and π⁡(Z,X)=Z[1]​Z[2]\pi(Z,X)=Z_{[1]}Z_{[2]}.

Proposition 10.

When Z[1],Z[2]∈{0,1}Z_{[1]},Z_{[2]}\in\{0,1\} are binary variables, for any 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}-PRWF π\pi, it holds that

ψ𝒮1,πo=𝔼⁡[𝕊0​[Y]​(1,1,X)−𝕊0​[Y]​(0,1,X)−𝕊0​[Y]​(1,0,X)+𝕊0​[Y]​(0,0,X)𝕊0​[A]​(1,1,X)−𝕊0​[A]​(0,1,X)−𝕊0​[A]​(1,0,X)+𝕊0​[A]​(0,0,X)],\displaystyle\psi_{\mathcal{S}_{1},\pi}^{o}=\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](1,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](0,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](1,0,X)+\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](0,0,X)}{\mathbb{S}_{0}[A](1,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[A](0,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[A](1,0,X)+\mathbb{S}_{0}[A](0,0,X)}\right],

where 𝕊0[Y](z1,z2,X)=𝔼[Y|Z[1]=z1,Z[2]=z2,X]\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](z_{1},z_{2},X)=\mathbb{E}[Y|Z_{[1]}=z_{1},Z_{[2]}=z_{2},X] and 𝕊0[A](z1,z2,X)=𝔼[A|Z[1]=z1,Z[2]=z2,X]\mathbb{S}_{0}[A](z_{1},z_{2},X)=\mathbb{E}[A|Z_{[1]}=z_{1},Z_{[2]}=z_{2},X] for z1,z2∈{0,1}z_{1},z_{2}\in\{0,1\}.

Proposition 10 gives an alternative representation of ψ𝒮1,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S}_{1},\pi}^{o}. If we interpret Z[1]Z_{[1]} as the group indicator and Z[2]Z_{[2]} as the time indicator, then ψ𝒮1,πo\psi_{\mathcal{S}_{1},\pi}^{o} reduces exactly to the IVDID functional studied in Ye et al. (41), though the underlying identification framework and nuisance functions might slightly differ from those in their work. For example, Definition 2.4(a) is equivalent to requiring that

𝔼[Y(0)∣Z[1]=1,Z[2]=1,X]−𝔼[Y(0)∣Z[1]=1,Z[2]=0,X]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z_{[1]}=1,Z_{[2]}=1,X]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z_{[1]}=1,Z_{[2]}=0,X]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z[1]=0,Z[2]=1,X]−𝔼[Y(0)∣Z[1]=0,Z[2]=0,X],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z_{[1]}=0,Z_{[2]}=1,X]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z_{[1]}=0,Z_{[2]}=0,X],

which is a conditional parallel trends restriction on the untreated potential outcome (41).

Moreover, when A=Z[1]​Z[2]A=Z_{[1]}Z_{[2]}, treatment is received only by units in the treated group (Z[1]=1Z_{[1]}=1) during the post-treatment period (Z[2]=1Z_{[2]}=1). The resulting functional further reduces to the classical difference-in-differences functional (1):

ψ𝒮1,πo=𝔼⁡[𝕊0​[Y]​(1,1,X)−𝕊0​[Y]​(0,1,X)−𝕊0​[Y]​(1,0,X)+𝕊0​[Y]​(0,0,X)].\displaystyle\psi_{\mathcal{S}_{1},\pi}^{o}=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](1,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](0,1,X)-\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](1,0,X)+\mathbb{S}_{0}[Y](0,0,X)\right].

Consequently, the 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV framework extends the IVDID functional in two important directions. First, it allows both the group index Z[1]Z_{[1]} and the time index Z[2]Z_{[2]} to be either discrete or continuous. Second, the PIV framework naturally accommodates multiple group indices, namely {Z[j]}j=1dZ\{Z_{[j]}\}_{j=1}^{d_{Z}} with dZ≥3d_{Z}\geq 3. In particular, when dZ=3d_{Z}=3, the triple-difference estimator proposed by Olden and Møen (28) can also be viewed as a special case of our framework.

τ^𝒮,π:=1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[{π⁡(Z,X)−ρ^𝒮,π(n,−k)​(Z,X)}​{A−δ^𝒮(n,−k)​(Z,X)}];\displaystyle\hat{\tau}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}:=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\hat{\rho}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{(n,-k)}(Z,X)\}\{A-\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-k)}(Z,X)\}];
τ^𝒮,∗:=1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[{A−δ^𝒮(n,−k)​(Z,X)}2−{A−π^∗(n,−k)​(Z,X)}2].\displaystyle\hat{\tau}_{\mathcal{S},*}:=\dfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}[\{A-\hat{\delta}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(n,-k)}(Z,X)\}^{2}-\{A-\hat{\pi}_{*}^{(n,-k)}(Z,X)\}^{2}].

Notably, the first two equations do not depend on τ𝒮,π\tau_{\mathcal{S},\pi} and τ𝒮,∗\tau_{\mathcal{S},*}, which are therefore replaced by “⋅\cdot” for simplicity. The variances of n​{β^𝒮,π−βo}\sqrt{n}\{\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}-\beta^{o}\} and n​{β^𝒮,∗−βo}\sqrt{n}\{\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},*}-\beta^{o}\} can be estimated by

1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[ϕ𝒮,π​(O,β^𝒮,π,α^𝒮,π(n,−k),τ^𝒮,π)2],1K​∑k=1K𝔼n​k​[ϕ𝒮,∗​(O,β^𝒮,∗,α^𝒮,∗(n,−k),τ^𝒮,∗)2],\displaystyle\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\!\left[\phi_{\mathcal{S},\pi}\!\left(O;\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},\pi},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}^{(n,-k)},\hat{\tau}_{\mathcal{S},\pi}\right)^{2}\right],\quad\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{nk}\!\left[\phi_{\mathcal{S},*}\!\left(O;\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},*},\hat{\alpha}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)},\hat{\tau}_{\mathcal{S},*}\right)^{2}\right],

respectively. Akin to Theorems 6 and 7, β^𝒮,π\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},\pi} and β^𝒮,∗\hat{\beta}_{\mathcal{S},*} are consistent and asymptotically normal, and their variance estimators are consistent. For a discussion of the estimation procedure when multiple 𝒮\mathcal{S}-PRWFs are used to identify βo\beta^{o}, we refer readers to Appendix B.

7 Simulation

We compare the proposed 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV estimator with several nonparametric and semiparametric methods, including the G-estimator (GE) (5) and the double machine learning method under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding (NUC) (6), where ZZ and XX are both included as measured confounders. For additional comparison, we also include several parametric methods, including sisVIVE (20) and TSHT (16) estimators. Specifically, the NUC method is implemented using the R package DoubleML, TSHT using RobustIV, and sisVIVE using sisVIVE.

We consider six DGPs under the invalid IV setting in Section 5. In all six DGPs, Z=(Z[1],Z[2],Z[3])∈𝒵:={−1,1}2×ℝZ=(Z_{[1]},Z_{[2]},Z_{[3]})\in\mathcal{Z}:=\{-1,1\}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}. The mechanisms for generating ZZ, AA, Y⁡(0)Y(0), and Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)Y(1)-Y(0) are summarized in Table 7.1. We independently generate U∼Uniform⁡(−1,1)U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1), X∼Uniform⁡(−0.5,0.5)X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-0.5,0.5), and the instrument disturbances ϵ[j]z∼Uniform⁡(−1,1)\epsilon_{[j]}^{z}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1) for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3. For the treatment mechanism in DGPs 3 and 4, we generate H∣X∼Bernoulli{0.7+0.3expit(−2X)},V=∑j=13Z[j]+ϵa,ϵa∼Uniform(−1,1),H\mid X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left\{0.7+0.3\mathrm{expit}(-2X)\right\},\;V=\sum_{j=1}^{3}Z_{[j]}+\epsilon^{a},\;\epsilon^{a}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1), where HH is conditionally exogenous given XX, expit⁡(t)=(1+e−t)−1\mathrm{expit}(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}.

In summary, Assumptions 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, and 5.4 hold under all DGPs, with νmax={2,3}\nu_{\max}=\{2,3\} for DGPs 1 and 2 and νmax={1,2,3}\nu_{\max}=\{1,2,3\} for DGPs 3–6. In addition, γmax=2\gamma_{\max}=2 in all six DGPs. Under each DGP, all IVs are mutually independent conditional on XX. In addition, the assumptions of sisVIVE and TSHT are satisfied under DGP 6, while the partially linear model in Equation (6.1) holds under DGPs 5 and 6.

Table 7.2 summarizes the motivation behind the design of these DGPs, each of which can be naturally represented by either Figure 5.1(a) or Figure 5.1(b). The true ATE is 22 in all six DGPs. We conduct the cross-fitting procedure with K=5K=5 folds and run 500 replications with sample size n=5,000n=5,000. In implementation, we omit the inner cross-fitting step and use the entire training sample I−kI_{-k} for both first-stage nuisance estimation and the subsequent estimation of κ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)\hat{\kappa}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)} and Γ^𝒮,∗(n,−k)\hat{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{S},*}^{(n,-k)}. To estimate the nuisance functions, the additive spline methods are employed to estimate 𝕊γ​[f]​(Z,X)\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[f](Z,X) for any f∈L2​(O)f\in L_{2}(O) using the R package mgcv (39).

The results are reported in Table 7.3. For notational brevity, the proposed estimators ψ^𝒮j,∗\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S}_{j},*} are denoted as PIVj for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3. Across all scenarios, we evaluate and compare the absolute value of bias (BIAS), standard deviation (SD), estimated standard error (SE), and empirical coverage rate (CR) of nominal 95% confidence intervals.

Overall, PIV1 and PIV2 perform stably, with small bias and low variance in moderate regimes. Moreover, their empirical coverage probabilities are close to the nominal 95% level, and the SDs generally match the SEs, suggesting well-calibrated variance estimation and confidence interval construction. By contrast, PIV3 (ψ^𝒮3,∗\hat{\psi}_{\mathcal{S}_{3},*}) shows substantial bias due to an overly aggressive choice of γ\gamma, which leads to an overestimation of the validity of the IVs.

The G-estimators (GE) proposed by Sun et al. (5) generally perform slightly worse than the PIV estimators. Their implementation is detailed in Appendix B. The bias of the GE method becomes particularly pronounced when 𝔼⁡[{π∗o​(Z,X)−𝕊γ​[A]​(Z,X)}2∣X]\mathbb{E}[\{\pi_{*}^{o}(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[A](Z,X)\}^{2}\mid X] and 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣X]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X] exhibit strong heterogeneity with respect to XX, especially in DGPs 1–4. This deterioration arises because the G-estimator effectively imposes a constant treatment effect assumption, which is violated under heterogeneous treatment effects.

The TSHT and sisVIVE estimators exhibit nonnegligible bias under DGPs 1–5, where both the plurality and majority rules are violated under DGPs 1, 2, 3, 5, and the treatment effect varies with the covariate XX under DGPs 1–4. Under DGP 6, the plurality rule holds, and TSHT achieves coverage close to the nominal 95% level. In summary, the results highlight the advantages of the PIV framework in terms of robustness and stability across a wide range of empirical environments.

Finally, the violin plots of the residual bias in Figure 7.1 show that PIV1 and PIV2 are centered close to zero across all DGPs, indicating small bias and stable performance. In contrast, PIV3, the GE estimators, NUC, TSHT, and sisVIVE exhibit noticeable bias in several settings.

8 Real data analysis

We apply our PIV method to the Australian Longitudinal Survey (ALS) data (23). The ALS is conducted annually from 1984 and collects information on the education, employment, earnings, and demographic characteristics of young Australians. We use the 1984 and 1985 waves as repeated cross-sectional data. The 1984 wave contains 2,403 individuals aged 15–24, while the 1985 wave contains 8,998 individuals aged 16–25. We are interested in estimating the ATE of having more than 12 years of education, compared with 12 years or fewer, on hourly wages.

Following Zhao and Cui (45), we construct hourly wages and years of education separately for the 1984 and 1985 waves. For the 1984 wave, the reported pay categories are converted into representative weekly monetary amounts, and the categories of weekly working hours are converted into representative numbers of hours. For the 1985 wave, reported earnings are converted to a weekly amount based on payment frequency. In both waves, hourly wages are calculated by dividing weekly earnings by weekly working hours. We exclude all individuals with missing hourly wages and impute the remaining missing values. The final dataset contains 5,661 individuals.

To construct the years of education, school-leaving grades are converted into years of schooling, while post-school qualifications are assigned between one and four additional years according to their type. We then compare this constructed value with the respondent’s reported years of schooling and retain the larger value. Finally, the education level is binarized at 12 years.

We include the survey wave indicator, residence in a capital city, birth in Australia, and attitudes toward the labor market in the PIV vector ZZ, with gender serving as the observed confounder XX. Residence in a capital city indicates whether the respondent had mostly lived in a capital city, while birth in Australia indicates whether the respondent was born in Australia. Attitudes toward women’s employment and gender roles are measured using a composite index constructed by summing responses to six survey questions, with higher values reflecting more egalitarian attitudes toward gender roles for women’s employment. Unlike Zhao and Cui (45), we retain the nonbinary attitude index, as our PIV framework accommodates nonbinary instruments.

Our choice of candidate PIV is motivated by the related IVDID literature (31; 45). These variables may be directly associated with wage levels and therefore may not satisfy the conventional exclusion restriction. However, IVDID allows such direct associations when they remain stable over time. In our PIV framework, this requirement is represented by the condition 𝔼[Y(0)∣Z,X]∈𝒮γ\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid Z,X]\in\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}, which allows the conditional mean of the hourly wage to depend on the candidate PIV through the structured function class 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}.

We compare our PIV framework with the G-estimator proposed by Sun et al. (5) and a method based on the no unmeasured confounding assumption, denoted by NUC. The NUC method is implemented using the double machine learning approach of Chernozhukov et al. (6). Specifically, the survey wave indicator, residence in a capital city, birth in Australia, attitudes toward the labor market, and gender are all treated as measured confounders. The results are summarized in Table 8.1.

In general, all methods produce positive point estimates, suggesting that having more than 12 years of education increases hourly wages. PIV3 and PIV4 are statistically significant at the 5% level, whereas PIV2 is significant only at the 10% level. The estimated values of PIV2\mathrm{PIV}_{2} and PIV3\mathrm{PIV}_{3} are close to each other, suggesting that ZZ might be an 𝒮γmax\mathcal{S}_{\gamma_{\max}}-PIV for AA with γmax=3\gamma_{\max}=3. The estimated value of PIV4\mathrm{PIV}_{4} differs substantially from that of PIV2\mathrm{PIV}_{2}, suggesting that PIV4\mathrm{PIV}_{4} is biased because not all the instruments are valid. The GE estimates also exhibit a similar pattern: GE4\mathrm{GE}_{4} yields a large and statistically significant estimate, whereas GE2\mathrm{GE}_{2} and GE3\mathrm{GE}_{3} yield smaller and statistically insignificant estimates.

The NUC method gives a smaller estimate of 1.66 with less uncertainty, although it relies on the absence of unmeasured confounding. Figure 8.1 further shows that the 95% confidence intervals for PIV3, PIV4, GE4, and NUC exclude zero, whereas those for PIV2, GE2, and GE3 include zero.

9 Discussion on invalid PIV

In this paper, we develop a novel projected instrumental variable framework for causal identification. By viewing conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework explores the use of more general projection operators. We also provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation and establish a connection between invalid IV and IVDID. Building on semiparametric efficiency theory, we have also developed debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference.

An important extension of the proposed framework is to accommodate invalid PIVs. One possible approach is to consider alternative formulations of the bridge Equation (3.2). We illustrate this approach with three examples below and leave the exploration of additional settings to future work.

1) Covariance-based moment conditions (22; 34). Specifically, let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a proper Hilbert subspace and consider finding a function ho​(X)h^{o}(X) that satisfies

𝔼[d(Z,X){Y−Aho(X)}{A−𝔼[A∣Z,X]}]=0,∀d∈𝒮⟂.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[d(Z,X)\{Y-Ah^{o}(X)\}\{A-\mathbb{E}[A\mid Z,X]\}\big]=0,\qquad\forall\,d\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp}. (9.1)

Notably, Equation (9.1) is analogous to the form considered in Equation (3.2). When 𝒮=L2​(X)\mathcal{S}=L_{2}(X), Equation (9.1) is equivalent to finding an ho​(X)h^{o}(X) such that Cov{π(Z,X),Cov{Y−Aho(X),A∣Z,X}∣X}≡0\mathrm{Cov}\{\pi(Z,X),\mathrm{Cov}\{Y-Ah^{o}(X),A\mid Z,X\}\mid X\}\equiv 0 for all π⁡(Z,X)\pi(Z,X). In particular, when ZZ is binary, ho​(X)h^{o}(X) can be solved in closed-form

ho​(X)=Cov{Z,Cov{Y,A∣Z,X}∣X}Cov{Z,Cov{A,A∣Z,X}∣X}.\displaystyle h^{o}(X)=\dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}\{Z,\mathrm{Cov}\{Y,A\mid Z,X\}\mid X\}}{\mathrm{Cov}\{Z,\mathrm{Cov}\{A,A\mid Z,X\}\mid X\}}.

Sun et al. (32) identify the ATE using 𝔼​[ho​(X)]\mathbb{E}[h^{o}(X)]. Therefore, the identification strategy adopted in Sun et al. (32) can be viewed as a special case of solving Equation (9.1).

2) Proximal causal inference with invalid proxies (43). Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z,X)L_{2}(Z,X), and find ho​(W,A,X)h^{o}(W,A,X) satisfying

𝔼⁡[d⁡(Z,A,X)​{Y−ho​(W,A,X)}]=0,∀d∈𝒮⟂,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[d(Z,A,X)\{Y-h^{o}(W,A,X)\}\big]=0,\qquad\forall\,d\in\mathcal{S}^{\perp},

where the orthogonal complement is taken in L2​(Z,A,X)L_{2}(Z,A,X), and Z,WZ,W are known as the treatment-inducing proxy and outcome-inducing proxy, respectively. When 𝒮=𝒮γ\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}, (43) identify the ATE using 𝔼⁡[ho​(W,1,X)−ho​(W,0,X)]\mathbb{E}[h^{o}(W,1,X)-h^{o}(W,0,X)].

3) Multiple PIVs are available, and some may be invalid. One can propose linear models and combine the projected idea with the majority and plurality rules (17; 20; 16). For example, suppose that XX is empty, and there exists a collection {ϕ1​(Z),…,ϕp​(Z)}\{\phi_{1}(Z),\ldots,\phi_{p}(Z)\} of linearly independent functions and a proper Hilbert subspace 𝒮\mathcal{S} such that 𝒮∩span⁡{ϕ1,…,ϕp}={0}\mathcal{S}\cap\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{p}\}=\{0\}. Define the partially linear subspace 𝒮pl:={s(Z)+∑i=1pθiϕi(Z):s∈𝒮,θ∈ℝp}\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pl}}:=\{s(Z)+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_{i}\phi_{i}(Z):s\in\mathcal{S},\ \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\}, a proper Hilbert subspace of L2​(Z)L_{2}(Z) induced by 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Assume the following outcome model

Y=βo​A+so​(Z)+∑i=1pθio​ϕi​(Z)+ϵ, with so∈𝒮 and 𝔼⁡[ϵ∣Z]=0, and we have\displaystyle Y=\beta^{o}A+s^{o}(Z)+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_{i}^{o}\phi_{i}(Z)+\epsilon,\text{ with $s^{o}\in\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid Z]=0$, and we have}
𝕊pl[Y](Z)=sYo(Z)+∑i=1pγioϕi(Z),𝕊pl[A](Z)=sAo(Z)+∑i=1pαioϕi(Z), where\displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{pl}}[Y](Z)=s_{Y}^{o}(Z)+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\gamma_{i}^{o}\phi_{i}(Z),\quad\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{pl}}[A](Z)=s_{A}^{o}(Z)+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}^{o}\phi_{i}(Z),\text{ where }
γio=θio+αio​βo, and ​sYo​(Z)=so​(Z)+βo​sAo​(Z)​ with ​sYo,sAo∈𝒮.\displaystyle\gamma_{i}^{o}=\theta_{i}^{o}+\alpha_{i}^{o}\beta^{o},\text{ and }s_{Y}^{o}(Z)=s^{o}(Z)+\beta^{o}s_{A}^{o}(Z)\text{ with }s_{Y}^{o},s_{A}^{o}\in\mathcal{S}.

Without loss of generality, assume that αio≠0\alpha_{i}^{o}\neq 0 for i=1,…,pi=1,\ldots,p, so that all candidate components are relevant to the treatment. Let 𝒱:={i:θio=0}\mathcal{V}:=\{i:\theta_{i}^{o}=0\}. The majority rule requires |𝒱|>p/2.|\mathcal{V}|>{p}/{2}. Therefore, βo\beta^{o} can be characterized as the value of β\beta that makes the vector {γio−αio​β}i=1p\left\{\gamma_{i}^{o}-\alpha_{i}^{o}\beta\right\}_{i=1}^{p} as sparse as possible. When 𝒮=ℝ\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}, this reduces to the model considered in Kang et al. (20).

Appendix

Appendix A Identification of other estimands

All the preceding discussion focuses on identifying the ATE. In this section, we consider several estimands beyond the ATE.

A.1 Mean potential outcome

We present the identification of the mean potential outcome 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a)]\mathbb{E}[Y(a)], where AA can be multi-categorical.

Assumption A.1 (ZZ-invariant counterfactual mean).

𝔼[Y(a)∣Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂Z[−ν0]∣X\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}\mid X.

Assumption A.2.

At least one of the two conditions holds:

  1. (a)

    (Additive IV) For some γ∈{1,…,|ν0|}\gamma\in\{1,\ldots,|\nu_{0}|\}, there exist {bν,a(U,Z[−ν],X):ν⊆ν0,|ν|=γ}\{b_{\nu,a}(U,Z_{[-\nu]},X):\nu\subseteq\nu_{0},\ |\nu|=\gamma\} and ca​(Z,X)c_{a}(Z,X) such that Pr⁡(A=a|Z,U,X)=∑ν⊆ν0,|ν|=γbν,a​(U,Z[−ν],X)+ca​(Z,X).\Pr(A=a\mid Z,U,X)=\sum_{\nu\subseteq\nu_{0},|\nu|=\gamma}b_{\nu,a}(U,Z_{[-\nu]},X)+c_{a}(Z,X).

  2. (b)

    (UU-invariant conditional counterfactual mean) 𝔼[Y(a)∣U,Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂U∣Z[−ν0],X\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X.

If condition (b) holds, define γ†,a​(ν0)=|ν0|\gamma_{\dagger,a}(\nu_{0})=|\nu_{0}|. Otherwise, define γ†,a​(ν0)\gamma_{\dagger,a}(\nu_{0}) as the largest γ∈{1,…,|ν0|}\gamma\in\{1,\ldots,|\nu_{0}|\} for which condition (a) holds.

Assumption A.1 states that 𝔼[Y(a)∣Z[−ν0],X]\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X] does not depend on Z[−ν0]Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}, paralleling the role of Assumption 5.3. Notably, under Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, and A.1, one can verify that 𝔼[Y(a)∣Z,X]\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid Z,X] does not depend on ZZ, thereby ruling out cases in which ZZ has a non-negligible effect on Y⁡(a)Y(a). Under the additional Assumption A.2(b), one can further verify that 𝔼[Y(a)∣A,U,Z,X]\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid A,U,Z,X] does not depend on AA, UU, or ZZ, thereby degenerating to the NUC setting. Compared to Chen et al. (1), the main novelty of Assumption A.2(a) lies in relaxing the restrictive additive IV assumption. We can now identify the mean potential outcome as follows.

Theorem 11 (Identification of mean potential outcome).

If Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, A.1, and A.2 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, and π\pi is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PRWF for the binary indicator I{A=a}I\{A=a\} with γ≤γ†,a​(ν0)\gamma\leq\gamma_{\dagger,a}(\nu_{0}), then

𝔼[Y(a)]=𝔼[π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊γ​[π]​(Z,X)𝔼[{π(Z,X)−𝕊γ[π](Z,X)}I{A=a}|X]I{A=a}Y].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(a)]=\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[\pi](Z,X)}{\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[\pi](Z,X)\right\}I\{A=a\}|X\right]}I\{A=a\}Y\right].

Following Chen et al. (1), this theorem can be extended to identify dose-response curves when the treatment AA is continuous.

A.2 Average treatment effect on the treated

In this subsection, we aim to identify the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), 𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣A=1]\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid A=1]. First, we reformulate Assumptions 5.3 and 5.4 as follows.

Assumption A.3 (ZZ-invariant treated counterfactual mean).

𝔼[Y(0)|A=1,Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂Z[−ν0]|X\mathbb{E}[Y(0)|A=1,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp Z_{[-\nu_{0}]}|X.

Assumption A.4.

At least one of the following conditions holds:

  1. (a)

    (Multiplicative IV) There exist two measurable functions b⁡(U,Z[−ν0],X)b(U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X) and c⁡(Z,X)c(Z,X) such that Pr⁡(A=1|Z,U,X)=b⁡(U,Z[−ν0],X)×c⁡(Z,X).\Pr(A=1\mid Z, U, X)=b(U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X)\times c(Z,X).

  2. (b)

    (UU-invariant treated counterfactual mean) 𝔼[Y(0)∣A=1,U,Z[−ν0],X]⟂⟂U∣Z[−ν0],X\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid A=1,U,Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X]\perp\!\!\!\perp U\mid Z_{[-\nu_{0}]},X.

We are now ready to establish identification of the ATT.

Theorem 12 (Identification of ATT).

Suppose that Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, A.3, and A.4 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, and π\pi is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PRWF with γ≤|ν0|\gamma\leq|\nu_{0}|. Then,

𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣A=1]=𝔼⁡[Y−𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊γ​[π]​(Z,X)}​(A−1)​Y∣X]𝔼⁡[{π⁡(Z,X)−𝕊γ​[π]​(Z,X)}​A|X]|A=1].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid A=1]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y-\dfrac{\mathbb{E}[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[\pi](Z,X)\}(A-1)Y\mid X]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\{\pi(Z,X)-\mathbb{S}_{\gamma}[\pi](Z,X)\}A\middle|X\right]}\middle|A=1\right].

When all the IVs are valid, Theorem 12 reduces to the identification strategy proposed in Liu et al. (4). In general, when |ν0|<dZ|\nu_{0}|<d_{Z}, Assumption A.4(a) relaxes the multiplicative IV assumption in Liu et al. (4).

Appendix C Uniqueness of the maximal regular index

In this section, we demonstrate the uniqueness of νmax\nu_{\max} defined in Section 5. In particular, we need the following regularity condition.

Assumption C.1.

For almost every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the conditional support of ZZ is a Cartesian product 𝒵⁡(x)=∏j=1dZ𝒵[j]​(x)\mathcal{Z}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{d_{Z}}\mathcal{Z}_{[j]}(x), and pZ|X​(z∣x)>0p_{Z\mid X}(z\mid x)>0 for every z∈𝒵⁡(x)z\in\mathcal{Z}(x).

We now present the following proposition.

Proposition 11.

Under Assumption C.1, let ν1\nu_{1} and ν2\nu_{2} be two index sets that satisfy Assumptions 5.1–5.4 (or 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, 5.4). Then, ν1∪ν2\nu_{1}\cup\nu_{2} is also an index set that satisfies the corresponding assumptions. In addition, if ν1⊆ν2\nu_{1}\subseteq\nu_{2}, then γ†​(ν1)≤γ†​(ν2)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{1})\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{2}).

By Proposition 11, if the family of regular index sets is nonempty, then it is closed under finite unions, and therefore has a unique largest element νmax\nu_{\max}. In addition, γ†​(νmax)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{\max}) is the largest value of γ†​(ν0)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}) over all regular index sets ν0\nu_{0}.

D.9 Proof of Proposition 9

Under Assumptions 5.1–5.4, the conditions required in Lemma 5.1(a) and (b) are satisfied for ν0\nu_{0}. Therefore, by Lemma 5.1(a), Definition 2.4(a) is satisfied for all γ≤|ν0|\gamma\leq|\nu_{0}|. By Lemma 5.1(b), Definition 2.4(b) is satisfied for all γ≤γ†​(ν0)\gamma\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}). As a result, ZZ is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV for all γ≤min⁡{|ν0|,γ†​(ν0)}=γ†​(ν0)\gamma\leq\min\{|\nu_{0}|,\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0})\}=\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}), since γ†​(ν0)≤|ν0|\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0})\leq|\nu_{0}| by the definition of γ†​(ν0)\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}). This completes the proof of Proposition 9(a).

If Assumptions 5.1, 5.2′, 5.3, and 5.4 hold for ν0\nu_{0}, Lemma 5.1(b) implies that Definition 2.4(b) holds for 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma} with all γ≤γ†​(ν0)\gamma\leq\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0}). Combining with the fact that Definition 2.4(a) holds for γ∗\gamma_{*}, we know that ZZ is an 𝒮γ\mathcal{S}_{\gamma}-PIV for all γ≤min⁡{γ∗,γ†​(ν0)}\gamma\leq\min\{\gamma_{*},\gamma_{\dagger}(\nu_{0})\}. This completes the proof of Proposition 9(b).
